name: Slowing speech and pausing

card.summary: Speaking slowly with deliberate pauses to sound calm, confident and authoritative.

quick.overview:
This is a delivery habit: slow the pace of speech and let pauses do the work.

People use it to sound more composed and authoritative.
quick.mechanism: Slower pacing and silences give words emphasis and signal calm, an element of delivery in classical rhetoric.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Overdoing pauses can feel stilted.

lead: Slowing speech and pausing is a delivery technique in which a person speaks at a measured pace and uses deliberate silences instead of filler words, so they come across as calm, confident and authoritative. The looks payoff is in presence: people use it to make their voice and delivery read as composed and self-assured, which is part of how a person is perceived alongside physical features.

Classical rhetoric counts delivery as one of the five canons, and Wikipedia's public speaking article describes it as including tone of voice, changes in pace, pauses, volume, body language and positioning [1]. Demosthenes is said to have practiced speaking while running to build breath control [1].

In a T Nation forum post, a member advised others not to fear silence, saying that fear of silence is where verbal pauses such as 'um', 'uh' and 'like' appear, and that these fillers sound worse than silence [2]. Another T Nation thread on public speaking offers confidence tips for people who were nervous speaking [3]. One PubMed-listed 2001 study, in the Journal of Social Psychology, examined gender and speech rate in the perception of competence and social attractiveness [4].

chain: Delivery that reads as calm and confident
angle.text: Slower pacing and silences replace filler words and rushed phrasing, which listeners tend to hear as composure. People use the habit to improve the impression their voice and manner give without any physical change [1][2].

infobox: Delivery, one of Cicero's five canons [1]

paras: The technique uses unhurried pacing, pauses before and after key points, and steady breath. Public-speaking references list pace and pauses among elements of delivery, along with tone, volume and body language [1]. Practice advice in forums includes replacing filler words with silence [2].

The 2001 Journal of Social Psychology study 'Gender and speech rate in the perception of competence and social attractiveness' set out to test whether listeners rate speakers who match their own speech rate as more competent; the available summary states its hypotheses rather than results [4].
It is discussed under voice and charisma as part of authority delivery, as a free habit that complements voice work and posture.
No studies found of slowing speech and pausing as an intervention for appearance or attractiveness; related research examines speech rate and listener perception of competence [4].

lore.intro: Pausing and slower speech come up in lifting and self-improvement forums as public-speaking and presence advice [2][3].

claims.claim: Silence sounds better than filler words
claims.believers: A T Nation member says fear of silence causes verbal pauses such as 'um' and 'like', and that fillers make a speaker sound worse than silence [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists pace and pauses as parts of speech delivery in classical rhetoric [1]; no study found tests fillers versus silence for perceived confidence.
